The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on near-term economic activity and pose downside risks; however, in line with the credit-channel literature (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch, 1996a; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist, 1994), the FOMC’s rapid cut to 0–0.25%, large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanded repos, discount-window easing, and dollar swap lines should reduce external finance premia, ease liquidity constraints, and support investment and spending. With market-based inflation compensation falling but survey-based expectations little changed, the literature on credible monetary policy and time inconsistency suggests expectations remain anchored, limiting deflation risk even as the Fed expands its balance sheet. While zero lower bound conditions raise liquidity-trap concerns, models emphasizing monetary policy’s role in stabilizing aggregate spending and the price level indicate these tools can still cushion the downturn. Overall tone: negative near term, mitigated by strong policy support.
